analysis.one_liner: Lets federal regulators block or roll back excessive health insurance rates and fine insurers that don't comply.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a single cosponsor, no hearing, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strengthen an Affordable Care Act rule that lets the government review health insurance rates. Today federal review mostly covers large premium increases; this bill would cover all rates and require HHS or state regulators to actually fix excessive, unjustified, or discriminatory rates before they take effect, using tools like rejecting rates, lowering rates, or ordering rebates. Insurers that refused to comply could face civil fines or lose their status as plans eligible for federal premium subsidies.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying individual and family health insurance, including plans sold on the ACA exchanges and older grandfathered plans, who would be protected from paying rates regulators judged excessive, unjustified, or unfairly discriminatory before those rates take effect.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who buy their own health insurance

how_it_helps.text: Requires corrective action — denying rates, modifying rates, or requiring consumer rebates — for excessive, unjustified, or unfairly discriminatory rates, before or as soon as possible after implementation [S2][S3].

Expands federal rate review, which currently covers only unreasonable premium increases, to cover all rate increases, including grandfathered plans that are otherwise largely exempt from ACA rules [S2][S3].
Lets HHS impose civil monetary penalties on insurers that ignore corrective actions and decertify plans as qualified health plans, which would make them ineligible for premium subsidies [S2][S3].
Allows HHS to step in and conduct reviews in state markets where the state regulator is not adequately doing the job, while leaving states free to impose stronger consumer protections [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance issuers, which could have rates denied or lowered, be ordered to pay rebates, and face fines or loss of subsidy-eligible plan status.

drawbacks.text: The bill shifts a traditionally state-run function toward federal control: HHS decides which markets the federal government reviews, which could displace state insurance commissioners' authority even in states that regulate rates well [S2][S3].

Tough rate enforcement has a real trade-off: suppressing premiums below what care costs can push insurers to exit markets or cut provider networks, reducing plan choice for consumers — a risk an honest supporter would have to weigh.
Decertifying plans from the exchanges as enforcement would mean those plans' customers lose access to premium subsidies, which could hurt the very consumers the bill aims to protect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is a real consumer protection: today federal rate review largely just flags big premium increases, but nothing in it forces rates to be corrected. Requiring rejection, modification, or rebates — with penalties behind it — would have teeth. The design is reasonably careful (it defers to states that do the job adequately), but the enforcement remedy of pulling a plan's subsidy eligibility could boomerang on its customers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the bill on March 9, 2020 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day; no further action was taken [S4][S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers are better off: they faced no new federal power to deny or roll back rates, order rebates, or fine noncompliance, and the existing review system that flags but does not correct rates stayed as is.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers who avoided new rate controls

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require corrective action on excessive, unjustified, or discriminatory health insurance rates

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No one voted on or against the bill and no opposition is on the record; the only recorded facts are a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would let federal or state regulators deny, lower, or order rebates on rates they judged excessive, unjustified, or discriminatory, and fine insurers that didn't comply. Insurers lose the ability to keep rates in place that no regulator would have forced them to correct — money that comes from consumers' premiums.

The bill preserves state authority and even lets states go further than federal rules, but it also lets HHS take over rate review in any state market where federal officials judge the state inadequate — a shift of turf toward Washington.
